ety.text: From Middle English that, from Old English þæt (“the, that”, neuter definite article and relative pronoun), from Proto-West Germanic *þat, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Cognate to Scots that, Saterland Frisian dät, West Frisian dat, Dutch dat, Low German dat and datt, German dass and das, Danish det, Swedish det, Icelandic það, Gothic 𐌸𐌰𐍄𐌰 (þata). Further from Proto-Indo-European *tód; compare Ancient Greek τό (tó), Sanskrit तद् (tád), Waigali ta, Lithuanian tai̇̃, Polish to.

senses.d: Introducing a clause that is the object of a verb, especially a reporting verb or verb expressing belief, knowledge, perception, etc.
ex: He told me that the book is a good read.
I believe that it is true.

senses.d: As delayed subject.
ex: It is almost certain that she will come.
It amazes me that people still believe this nonsense.

senses.d: As direct subject.
ex: That she will come is almost certain.
That people still believe this nonsense amazes me.

senses.d: Introducing the complement of a mandative verb.
ex: I insist that you come.
The boss ordered that the worker enter the room.

senses.d: Introducing a clause that complements an adjective or passive participle.
ex: I'm sure that you are right.
She is convinced that he is British.

senses.d: Expressing a reason or cause: because, in that.
ex: Be glad that you have enough to eat.
I was saddened that you felt so little for me.

senses.d: Introducing a subordinate clause modifying an adverb.
ex: Was John there? — Not that I saw.
How often did she visit him? — Twice that I saw.

senses.d: Introducing a clause that describes the information content of a preceding reporting noun.
ex: I heard a rumour that they got married.
Reports that he left the country are circulating.

senses.d: Introducing — especially, but not exclusively, with an antecedent like so or such — a subordinate clause expressing a result, consequence, or effect.
ex: The noise was so loud that she woke up.
The problem was sufficiently important that it had to be addressed.

senses.d: Introducing a subordinate clause that expresses an aim, purpose, or goal (“final”), and usually contains the auxiliaries may, might, or should: so, so that, in order that.
ex: He fought that others might have peace.
When hungry Judges ſoon the Sentence ſign, / And Wretches hang that Jury-men may Dine; […]

senses.d: The (thing, person, idea, etc) indicated or understood from context, especially if more remote physically, temporally or mentally than one designated as “this”, or if expressing distinction.
ex: That book is a good read. This one isn't.
That battle was in 1450.

senses.d: The thing, person, idea, quality, event, action, or time indicated or understood from context, especially if more remote geographically, temporally or mentally than one designated as “this”, or if expressing distinction.
ex: That's my car over there.
He went home, and after that I never saw him again.

senses.d: Used to refer to a noun phrase or statement just made.
ex: They're getting divorced. What do you think about that?
They gave me the book about whales. That I've not yet read.

senses.d: Used to emphatically affirm or deny a previous statement or question.
ex: The water is so cold! — That it is.
Would you like another piece of cake? — That I would!

senses.d: In a relative clause, referring to a previously mentioned noun, as subject, direct object, indirect object, or object of a preposition; which, who.
ex: I didn't see the car that hit me.
The CPR course that she took really came in handy.

senses.d: Used in place of relative adverbs such as where or when; often omitted.
ex: the place that [= where or to which] I went last year
the last time that [= when] I went to Europe

senses.d: Denoting an equal degree.
ex: Here's the measurement – the ribbon must be that long, no longer and no shorter.

senses.d: Denoting ‘as much’, ‘no less’.
ex: She said we waited for three hours, but I'm sure it wasn't that long.
It didn't seem like ten miles, but actually it was that far.

senses.d: To a great extent or degree; very, particularly.
ex: I was seen quite quickly — I didn't have to wait that long.
I did the run last year, and it wasn't that difficult.

senses.d: To such an extent; so.
ex: Ooh, I was that happy I nearly kissed her.
This was carried with that little noise that for a good space the vigilant Bishop was not awak'd with it.

senses.d: Something being indicated that is there; one of those.

grp.label: to a given extent or degree

ety.text: From Middle English than, thanne (“than; then”), from Old English þanne, a variant of þonne (“then; when; than”), from Proto-West Germanic *þannē, an alteration of *þan (“then; than”), from Proto-Germanic *þan (“then; than”), from earlier *þam, from Proto-Indo-European *tóm, accusative masculine of *só (“that”, demonstrative pronoun). Cognate with Dutch dan (“then; than”), German denn (“for; so”), German dann (“then”). Doublet of then.

senses.d: Used in comparisons, to introduce the basis of comparison.
ex: The artist worried more than was necessary: there were a lot of people at the exhibition, more than came last year.
Profits were higher than forecast.

senses.d: Because; for.

Introduces a comparison, and is associated with comparatives, and with words such as more, less, and fewer. Typically, it seeks to measure the force of an adjective or similar description between two predicates.
ex: Patients diagnosed more recently are probably surviving an average of longer than two years.
No player is more skillful than Greg.

senses.d: At that time; then.

ety.text: From Middle English thanken (“to express gratitude, give thanks; to congratulate, rejoice with, or wish joy to; to extol, praise; to hold responsible for”), from Old English þancian, þoncian (“to thank”), from Proto-West Germanic *þankōn, from Proto-Germanic *þankōną (“to thank”), from *þankaz (see etymology 1) + *-ōną (suffix forming infinitives of verbs from nouns).

senses.d: To express appreciation or gratitude toward (someone or something).
ex: She thanked him for the lift.
I can eate no meate, I thanke you.

senses.d: In the future tense in the form one will thank someone to do something, chiefly expressing a command or criticism: to request that (someone) do something.
ex: I’ll thank you not to smoke in my house!

senses.d: To express appreciation or gratitude for (something).
To respond to (someone) out of, or as if out of, appreciation or gratitude.
ex: I should summon my lord from the Queen's royal presence to do your business, should I?—I were like to be thanked with a horse-whip.

senses.d: Chiefly followed by for: to credit or hold (someone or something) responsible, especially for something negative; to blame.
ex: We can thank global warming for this freak weather.

senses.d: To express gratitude.

grp.label: to express appreciation or gratitude toward (someone or something)

Inherited from Old Spanish agradesçer, equivalent to a- + grado (“will; liking, preference”) + -ecer. Cognate with Aragonese agradeixer and Catalan agrair.
From a- + grado + -ecer.

From Middle English thanks, thankes, from Old English þancas (“thanks”), from Proto-Germanic *þankōs, nominative plural of *þankaz (“thought, gratitude”), from Proto-Indo-European *teng- (“to think, feel”). More at thank.

senses.d: Used to express appreciation or gratitude.
ex: Could you give me a hand, please? — Yes, sure. — Thanks. —Have you got enough now? —Yes, thanks.
Would you like some potatoes? — Thanks. —How many?

senses.d: An expression of appreciation or gratitude.
ex: After all I’ve done, a simple acknowledgment is the thanks I get?

senses.d: Grateful feelings or thoughts; favour, goodwill, graciousness.

ety.text: From Middle French merci, mercy, from Old French merci, from Latin mercēdem (“wages, fee, price”). Used as an interjection of gratitude since at least the early 12th century, originally as grand merci, for instance spelled granz merciz in Li coronemenz Looïs.
Plural of grazia (“grace”), from Latin grātia, as used in the phrase grātiās agō (“to thank; to express thanks”). Compare Sicilian grazzi and Spanish gracias.
From gracia < Latin grātia, as used in the phrase gratias agere (“to express thanks”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Latin obligātus (“obliged”), past participle of obligō (“to bind in obligation”).

From Middle English thankful, from Old English þancful, þancfull (“thoughtful, pleasing, agreeable, pleasant, thankful, grateful”), equivalent to thank + -ful. Compare Old High German undankfol (“unthankful, ungrateful”).

senses.d: Showing appreciation or gratitude.
ex: I'm thankful that you helped me out today. How can I ever repay you?

senses.d: Obtaining or deserving thanks; thankworthy.
